summary:
Cusco stands under the national framework of Peru. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, trans identity is not an offence, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. No department-level trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding could be located for Cusco; every binding rule below applies in Cusco as elsewhere in Peru.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, but Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage; the repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025, with exceptions for custody, medical need, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the bill, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in a legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP also invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020–2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty, including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom restriction's practical burden falls unevenly on visitors: enforcement depends on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, which can out a trans traveller at the point of entry in hotels, malls, transport hubs and public buildings across Cusco. Gianna Camacho's warning on this point is a general one and applies wherever the law is enforced.

Peru's record on anti-LGBT violence sits alongside a documented pattern of state involvement: the Observatorio figures include state violence among the 170 rights-violation cases, and the Azul Rojas Marín case was perpetrated by police officers. A trans visitor can therefore expect the risk to come from official actors as well as the public.

Cusco's status as a major international tourist destination concentrates visitors in transit spaces (Jorge Chávez airport in Lima is the entry point for most) where the restroom restriction and ID-check exposure are most likely to be encountered first.

Compared with neighbouring South American states, Peru's absence of LGBT anti-discrimination coverage places it with Paraguay and Guyana rather than with the majority of the region.
localsOnly:

Trans residents may change their legal name, and since the Constitutional Court's 21 October 2016 ruling (published 8 November) may change gender markers on national identity documents through a judicial process without surgery. MINSA's June 2024 revision of 'transsexualism' to 'gender discordance' and removal of pathologising terminology from health guidance affect insurance classification and clinical practice for residents; conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals.

outOfScopeNotes:
No department-level (región Cusco) trans-specific law, municipal ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding was located in the source inventory; all sources are national in scope. Whether Cusco regional or municipal authorities have issued any guidance implementing Law 32331 is unresolved and not sourced here.

The number of bills is stated inconsistently across sources: the parent framework cites 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, while Infobae cites 6506 and 8457. Which bill number is correct is unresolved.

The current summary states the ban 'stood at committee stage in February 2025'; the IDEHPUCP source records plenary approval on 2 April 2025 and the parent framework records enactment as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025. The legislative sequence is treated here as committee approval in February, plenary approval in April, enactment in May, per the dated sources.

Whether the exceptions listed in the February 2025 committee version survived into Law 32331 as enacted is not sourced.

Whether the Gender Identity Law introduced in 2016 has advanced after March 2021 is unresolved.
